visuals.title: Tumours to think of
visuals.text: Lung, breast, renal cancer and myeloma; bone is where calcium is released.

visual.title: Adjusted calcium
visual.label: 3.2: rehydrate IV
visual.caption: Under 3.0 and asymptomatic: stop calcium-raising drugs and drink fluids.

glossary.Serum calcium: The level of calcium measured in the liquid part of the blood.
glossary.Osteoclast-mediated: Carried out by osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone.
glossary.Tumour: An abnormal growth of cells; here a cancer.
glossary.Secretion: Release of a substance from a cell.
glossary.Bone metastases: Cancer that has spread to the bones from somewhere else.
glossary.Lung cancer: Cancer arising in the lung, a common cause of hypercalcaemia.
glossary.Breast cancer: Cancer of the breast; often spreads to bone.
glossary.Kidney stones: Hard deposits, often calcium, that form in the kidney and can cause severe flank pain.
glossary.Bone pain: Deep aching from bone, here from resorption or metastases.
glossary.Confusion: Difficulty thinking clearly, a sign of significant hypercalcaemia.
glossary.Muscle weakness: Reduced strength, as high calcium dampens nerve and muscle excitability.
glossary.Dehydration: Loss of body water, here from calcium-driven polyuria.
glossary.Constipation: Infrequent or hard stools; high calcium slows gut movement.
glossary.Suppressed: Switched off, so the level is low.
glossary.Parathyroid: Four small glands behind the thyroid that make PTH to control calcium.
glossary.Acute kidney injury: A sudden fall in kidney function.
glossary.Coma: Deep unconsciousness from which the patient cannot be woken.
glossary.Confirmatory test: A test that proves the suspected diagnosis.
glossary.Inappropriately normal: A normal value that should be low given the situation, so still abnormal.
glossary.ECG: Electrocardiogram: a recording of the heart's electrical activity.
glossary.Cancer work-up: Tests to find the type and spread of a suspected cancer.
glossary.Vitamin D: A vitamin that raises calcium absorption from the gut.
glossary.IV: Intravenous: given directly into a vein.
glossary.0.9% saline: Normal saline, a salt solution used for IV fluid replacement.
glossary.Osteoclast activity: How much bone the osteoclasts are breaking down.
glossary.Contraindicated: Should not be used because it could cause harm.
glossary.RANKL inhibitor: A drug blocking RANKL, the signal that switches on osteoclasts.
glossary.Steroids: Corticosteroid drugs such as prednisolone; here they reduce calcium, especially in myeloma.
glossary.Receptor: A protein a hormone binds to in order to act on a cell.
glossary.Renal calcium reabsorption: The kidney taking calcium back into the blood instead of losing it in urine.
glossary.Phosphate reabsorption: The kidney taking phosphate back into the blood.
glossary.Axis: A hormone control loop, here calcium sensing and PTH output.
glossary.Cytokines: Signalling proteins released by cells, here to activate osteoclasts.
glossary.Monoclonal antibody: A lab-made antibody that targets one specific molecule.
glossary.Osteoclast maturation: The development of immature cells into active bone-dissolving osteoclasts.
glossary.Renally safe: Safe in kidney disease because it is not cleared by the kidneys.
glossary.Cardiac action potential: The electrical cycle of a heart muscle cell during each beat.
